books.section: Topic 8.7 America as a World Power
Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

primary_sources: R. S. Norris and H. M. Kristensen, 'Global Nuclear Stockpiles, 1945-2002,' Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (2002)

source: original; stimulus table from Norris and Kristensen, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (2002), via Our World in Data

stimulus.source_note: Warhead counts: R. S. Norris and H. M. Kristensen, 'Global Nuclear Stockpiles, 1945-2002,' Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (2002), via Our World in Data. Figures are approximate.
stimulus.text:
Nuclear warheads held, by year (approximate)

| Year | United States | Soviet Union |
| 1949 | 235 | 1 |
| 1955 | 2,422 | 200 |
| 1960 | 18,638 | 1,627 |
| 1965 | 31,139 | 6,144 |

stem: The pattern in the table best supports which conclusion about the arms race?

options.text: Only the United States built nuclear weapons in these years
options.misconception: The table shows the Soviet total rising from 1 warhead in 1949 to 6,144 in 1965.

options.text: The Soviet Union stopped building nuclear weapons after 1955
options.misconception: The table shows the Soviet total rising from 200 in 1955 to 1,627 in 1960 and 6,144 in 1965.

options.text: Both sides built arsenals larger than needed to destroy each other
The arsenals of both countries shrank steadily through these years
options.misconception: The table shows both totals rising in every year shown, not shrinking.

rationales.A: The table shows the Soviet total rising from 1 warhead in 1949 to 6,144 in 1965, so both sides built weapons.
rationales.B: The table shows the Soviet total rising after 1955, to 1,627 in 1960 and 6,144 in 1965.
rationales.C: Background from the books: by the early 1960s the United States held enough weapons to destroy the world several times over, and the Soviet arsenal kept growing beside it.
rationales.D: The table shows both totals rising in every year shown, not shrinking.
rationales.general:
1. Both columns grow steeply: the American total rises from 235 to more than 31,000.
2. The Soviet total rises too, from 1 to more than 6,000.
3. Background from the books: by the early 1960s the United States alone held enough weapons to destroy the world several times over.
4. Two arsenals that big go far beyond what either side needed to destroy the other.
Remember: when both sides keep building past any sensible need, the race itself is the point.
